li.a: Al Jazeera: Children massacred in Pakistan school attack
Al Jazeera: Remembering the Peshawar school massacre
BBC News: Pakistan Taliban: Peshawar school attack leaves 141 dead
The Guardian: Peshawar school massacre: 'This is Pakistan's 9/11 - now is the time to act'
Human Rights Watch: Dreams Turned into Nightmares: Attacks on Students, Teachers, and Schools in Pakistan

content.p: On the morning of Tuesday 16 December 2014, armed men from the Pakistani Taliban entered the Army Public School in Peshawar, a military-run school in the north-west of Pakistan, and began shooting the people inside it. By the evening the army was reporting 141 dead, among them 132 children and nine members of staff. Later accounts put the toll higher: Al Jazeera's anniversary feature said 144 people were killed, Human Rights Watch said 145, and a Pakistani editor writing in The News said 147. The attackers were all killed. It was the deadliest attack by an armed group in Pakistan's history, according to Al Jazeera.

The Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) claimed responsibility the same day. Pakistan responded by ending a pause on executions in terrorism cases, by setting up military courts, and, years later, by a judicial inquiry into how an army-run school came to be so poorly defended.
content.h2: A school in a high-security zone
content.p: The school stood on Warsak Road in Peshawar, a city close to the Afghan border that, in the BBC's words, had seen some of the worst violence of the Taliban insurgency. It stood near a military complex, and many of its pupils were the children of military personnel; the BBC said most would have been 16 or younger. Al Jazeera noted that families who were not connected to the army also sent their children to military schools because of their relatively high standard of education.

The attack came six months into Operation Zarb-e-Azb, the army's campaign against the TTP and its allies in North Waziristan, which began on 15 June 2014. The military said it had retaken large areas and killed more than 1,270 fighters. It was also running an operation in the Khyber tribal agency next to Peshawar. Al Jazeera's report described the school as a soft target with relatively low security, even though it lay inside a high-security part of central Peshawar.

Military officials said about 1,100 students and teachers were at the school when the attack began at around 10:30 a.m. Bajwa, the army spokesman, told reporters that every attacker was wearing a suicide vest and carrying supplies for days, yet the gunmen fired without discrimination and did not appear to be planning a hostage-taking. The BBC wrote that it appeared the militants had scaled walls to get into the compound and set off a bomb at the start of the assault. Al Jazeera reported that the attackers wore paramilitary uniforms.

Survivors told reporters that the gunmen went from classroom to classroom. Shahrukh Khan, a pupil, told the BBC that a gunman came into his classroom and opened fire at random; hiding under a desk, he watched friends being shot and saw two teachers killed. He told Al Jazeera that he was shot in both legs and survived by lying still and pretending to be dead. Another boy told reporters he had been with a group of ten friends who tried to run and hide, and that he was the only one of them to survive. The BBC and Al Jazeera gave Shahrukh Khan's age differently, as 17 and 16.

Al Jazeera's correspondent in Peshawar, Kamal Hyder, said most of the younger pupils escaped while the senior students were less fortunate. Al Jazeera quoted a TTP spokesman, Muhammad Khorasani, as saying the attackers had been ordered to let the youngest children leave and to kill the rest. Al Jazeera's anniversary feature told the day through the chemistry teacher Andaleeb Aftab, who barricaded herself with three colleagues in a staff-room bathroom for nearly eight hours while she listened to the shooting. When soldiers rescued her she asked first about her three children, all pupils at the school. Two were unhurt. Her eldest, 16-year-old Huzaifa, had been shot five times and was dead.

A heavy contingent of security forces reached the school soon after the attack began and started a rescue operation, according to Al Jazeera's report. Later in the day, reports spoke of as many as ten loud explosions at the school, which reporters read as the operation reaching a climax. Officials told Al Jazeera that all seven attackers had been killed. A hospital doctor told the BBC that many of the injured children had head and chest wounds, and the BBC's pictures showed coffins stacked at a Peshawar hospital.

The TTP said in a statement that the attack was in retaliation for Operation Zarb-e-Azb. Al Jazeera reported that the TTP said many of its members' relatives had been killed in the campaign and that the school attack was revenge for those deaths; its correspondent added that the group's members wanted to inflict pain. He told the BBC that the militants had been forced to act because of army attacks. Human Rights Watch quoted him as saying the attack was meant to make the army feel the pain of what he called the targeting of the group's families and women.

The group also released a video in which, Al Jazeera reported, its leader Maulana Fazlullah said that the fighters had attacked the school and killed the children of army personnel, not civilians, and that such people would always be targets. The group warned of more attacks to come.

Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif called the attack a "national tragedy" and spoke of the dead as "my children". US President Barack Obama said the attackers had "once again shown their depravity", and UN Secretary General Ban Ki-moon called it "an act of horror and rank cowardice". Malala Yousafzai, who had received the Nobel Peace Prize six days earlier, said she and millions of others would mourn the dead children as her "brothers and sisters". The opposition leader Imran Khan called the attack "utter barbarism".
Outside Peshawar's hospitals parents waited for news. The BBC reported a woman, Irshadah Bibi, who had lost her 12-year-old son, beating her face in grief and throwing herself against an ambulance.

A BBC analysis called the attack a possible watershed for a country long accused of treating some militants as strategic assets. A Guardian collection of reactions from Pakistanis a few days later suggested a change of mood. A respondent in Islamabad said that the old mixture of hatred and fear of the Taliban had given way to anger strong enough to remove the fear, and another respondent called it "Pakistan's 9/11 moment".
content.h2: Executions, military courts and the National Action Plan
content.p: Sharif lifted the moratorium on the death penalty in terrorism cases and said there would no longer be a difference between "good" and "bad" Taliban, the Guardian reported. Some Pakistanis the paper quoted thought the step was merely for show; others said it was what the public wanted. The Guardian added that on the Friday after the attack Pakistani forces began air and ground operations in the Khyber agency, killing 59 militants.

Sharif also announced a 20-point National Action Plan against terrorism. Human Rights Watch noted that none of its 20 points concerned students or education, and that the government had paid little attention to protecting schools until the attack. Afterwards the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government set aside 7.5 billion Pakistani rupees for the security of government schools in January 2015, and other measures included training teachers to use arms, mock security drills and higher boundary walls. Al Jazeera reported that some teachers felt safer for being armed while others said a teacher's job was only to teach.

Human Rights Watch also criticised the secret military courts that the government set up after the attack. Families, it said, could not know whether the real perpetrators had been punished, because the trials were held in secret. In December 2015 four men who a military court had found guilty of providing money, transport and other help to the attackers were executed in a prison in Kohat. The News described them as four men from Peshawar and Khyber who had been arrested in December 2015 for allegedly facilitating the six terrorists, and reported that the parents were not satisfied. They argued that the masterminds had still to be caught and punished, and that those guilty of neglect in protecting the school should be identified.

Schools across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa closed for nearly a month, according to Al Jazeera. The Punjab government closed all its schools and announced winter holidays from 19 December 2014 until 12 January 2015, according to Human Rights Watch. The Army Public School went back to work on Monday 12 January 2015, said the teacher Mahrukh Qayyum, who had been teaching a fifth-grade class when the gunfire began; at first she took it for an army drill. She named former pupils she had taught who died, together with teachers and staff, among them Hafsa Khushk, Beenish Pervez, Salma Tariq and Professor Tahira Qazi.

A year later parents spoke of fear and trauma. Tahir Aneez Malik, whose 14-year-old son Hammad was killed, said the children were afraid it could happen again. His daughter Kashaf, 12, who survived the attack, was back at the school, where security had been increased. Andaleeb Aftab had returned to teach in the classroom where her son had sat, with his name still on the notice boards.

Bereaved parents protested for years, believing that the people responsible had not been caught. According to The News they split into at least two groups, and some of them called the attack a "target-killing" rather than an act of terrorism. The Supreme Court of Pakistan, under then Chief Justice Mian Saqib Nisar, took notice of the case at the parents' request. In October 2018 it asked the Peshawar High Court to set up a judicial commission. The commission was a single judge, Justice Mohammad Ibrahim Khan.

After nearly 20 months, in which it recorded statements from 132 people, 31 of them army and police officials, the commission produced a report of 525 pages. By The News's account, it found that the security guards at the school were not properly positioned to hold the attackers off and give time for the Quick Response Force and the Rapid Response Force, which were rushed to the scene. It said the security patrol near the school was misled by the attackers, who set their vehicle on fire to draw its attention and entered at the rear. Senior army officials had said at the time that most of the troops available in Peshawar had been sent to North Waziristan for Zarb-e-Azb and the Khyber operation. The commission praised the armed forces for their sacrifices, but wrote that the incident had "plagued their success stories" which "deserved deification". It accepted that terrorism in Pakistan had peaked in 2013 and 2014, but said this did not oblige it to hold that sensitive installations and soft targets could be abandoned to terrorists.

The commission also cited the porous Afghan border and unrestricted movement of Afghan refugees as a reason the attackers were able to get in. On the warning that the National Counter Terrorism Authority had issued, it said the alert was generic, about terrorists seeking to target army families and academic institutions in retaliation for the military operations. It noted that some people found guilty of negligence, including army personnel, had already been punished.

Chief Justice Gulzar Ahmed later ordered the government to make the report public and to give a copy, with the government's response to it, to the parents. In court he regretted that lower-ranked officials were traditionally held responsible while those in senior positions were spared. He said that the militants had achieved their objective and that the security institutions should have been aware of the conspiracy.
content.h2: The men blamed for planning it
content.p: The News wrote that two masterminds of the attack, both in Afghanistan and members of the TTP, were killed in US drone strikes. Khalifa Umar Mansoor, also known as Umar Naray, who had claimed responsibility and was seen in photographs with the attackers as they set out for Pakistan, was killed on 9 July 2016 in Nangarhar province. Maulana Fazlullah, the TTP's head, who the writer said must have known of the planning and who had defended the attack, was killed on 14 June 2018 in Kunar province. The writer suggested that these deaths may have brought some closure to relatives, while the commission's report tried to answer some of their questions.
